learn.canDo: Design tool schemas and sets a model uses reliably, and keep the number of tools in view small with retrieval.
learn.why: Tool design decides whether an agent works. Interviewers ask how you would prevent wrong-tool and bad-argument failures.
learn.keyIdea: The model requests; your code validates and executes.

learn.canDo: Explain the loop, compute why cost grows with the square of the steps, and cap steps and cost sensibly.
learn.why: Runaway agent bills are the classic production story. Knowing why they grow quadratically shows real understanding.
learn.keyIdea: Every turn re-reads everything before it.

learn.canDo: Describe ReAct's thought-action-observation cycle and why it beats answering from memory or acting blindly.
learn.why: ReAct is the root of most agent designs. Naming what each alternative lacks is a standard question.
learn.keyIdea: Thinking needs something to think about.

learn.canDo: Compute the success of a fixed plan as a product of steps, and add bounded replanning to make long tasks reliable.
learn.why: Long agent tasks fail by compounding. Bounded replanning is the standard remedy.

learn.canDo: Layer a recent window, a summary, pinned facts and retrieval to remember a long conversation within a token budget.
learn.why: Memory is a selection problem, and the layered answer is what separates a demo from a product.

learn.canDo: Name the main agent failure modes and defend against loops, bad tool calls and silent wrong answers.
learn.why: Agents fail in ways ordinary software does not. Layered limits and tracing are the practical answer.
learn.keyIdea: The loop will never decide to stop on its own.

learn.canDo: Gate agent actions by consequence, make low-risk mistakes reversible, and avoid approval fatigue.
learn.why: Putting a human in the loop is easy; putting them where they help is the skill.

learn.canDo: Choose a workflow, an agent, or a router between them based on how predictable the task is.
learn.why: Not every task needs an agent. Starting simple and routing by need is the advice teams most often wish they had taken.

learn.canDo: Split a task across parallel workers with clean contexts, and weigh the quality gain against coordination cost.
learn.why: Research agents use this pattern. The knee in the quality curve is the detail interviewers look for.
learn.keyIdea: Small clean contexts, and a cost to combine them.

learn.canDo: Choose sectioning or voting, size a vote, and use a quorum to avoid the tail latency of the slowest call.
learn.why: Parallel calls help accuracy and speed and hurt cost and tail latency. Quorums are the standard fix.
learn.keyIdea: Divide for speed, repeat for certainty.

learn.canDo: Compare supervisor, debate and swarm organisations on quality, tokens and failures.
learn.why: Multi-agent designs are fashionable and costly. Reasoning about their communication cost shows judgement.

learn.canDo: Contain a runaway agent with layered limits, a consequence-based gate, idempotent tools and an independent alert.
learn.why: A runaway agent tests every agent safeguard at once. The skill is knowing which control stops what.
learn.keyIdea: Bound the loop, gate the damage, alert independently.

chapter.story: Pigeon's assistant starts taking actions, not just writing answers, and the team learns what that costs.
outcomes: Design tools and loops that work and stay bounded
Plan, remember and verify across long tasks
Put people where mistakes cannot be undone
Choose between workflows, agents and teams of agents
chapter.why: An agent is a model with permission to act. Every capability here comes with a way to fail, and each safeguard removes one.
chapter.payoff: In an interview you can design an agent and say how it fails and what bounds it. At work you will review an agent design for loops, scope and cost.
